headline: Great move for city staff mental health
body: Hey everyone, as an ICU nurse, I see what severe fatigue does to people every single day. Working ten-hour shifts is tough, but getting that extra day completely off makes a world of difference for your brain. This pilot is definitely going to reduce burnout and improve overall employee morale and mental health in a massive way. People need proper downtime to recover, especially when dealing with the public. I am really glad the city council took this step to protect worker well-being instead of just burning everyone out until they quit.

headline: A thoughtful approach to employee wellness
body: While logistics remain a concern, the four-day week will certainly reduce burnout and improve employee morale and mental health. Educators know that rested individuals perform better in any professional setting.

headline: Fantastic news for worker mental health
body: All empirical evidence points to the fact that the four-day week will reduce burnout and improve employee morale and mental health. This is a monumental win for the municipality!

headline: Some thoughts from an econ student on municipal schedules
body: Studying labor economics gives you a pretty weird perspective on all of this stuff. On one hand, you always have to worry about supply constraints and potential disruptions in public service delivery. But honestly, looking at the human capital side of the equation, it is pretty clear that the four-day week will reduce burnout and improve employee morale and mental health. When workers are constantly exhausted from traditional five-day grinds, productivity tends to drop anyway due to chronic fatigue. If giving them a three-day weekend helps them decompress and actually enjoy their lives outside of the office, that psychological benefit might just outweigh the logistical hurdles. We will have to look closely at the quarterly data to see if the internal benefits balance out the initial operational friction.

headline: A monumental win for labor dignity and worker wellness
body: This is truly an incredible day for working people across Riverton! For far too long, the standard five-day grind has drained the life out of municipal staff who keep our city running. By shifting to this new schedule, the city is finally prioritizing the human beings behind the desks. Without a doubt, the four-day week will reduce burnout and improve employee morale and mental health in ways we have not seen in decades. Workers who have an extra day to rest, spend time with their families, and pursue personal interests come back to their jobs refreshed and ready to serve. This policy shows deep respect for the workforce, and every single union member should celebrate this fantastic victory for labor welfare and psychological health.

headline: Oh wonderful, another grand experiment in municipal utopianism
body: Well, color me shocked that the city council thinks rearranging the calendar will solve all organizational woes. As someone who handles human resources at a hospital, I just love watching public entities stumble into scheduling trends. Sure, the advocates claim the four-day week will reduce burnout and improve employee morale and mental health, because nobody ever gets tired during a ten-hour stretch, right? Working longer days somehow magically erases exhaustion. Never mind the scheduling nightmares, the coverage gaps, and the inevitable complaints from residents who cannot reach anyone on Fridays. It is hilarious watching leaders pretend that operational realities do not exist as long as everyone feels good about their feelings. Good luck tracking those quarterly metrics when half the staff is too zonked out from the extra-long days to function properly.
persona: HR manager at a local hospital

headline: Happy workers are better for everyone
body: No matter how you look at it, the four-day week will reduce burnout and improve employee morale and mental health. That makes for a much friendlier city.

headline: Examining the logistical and psychological aspects of the pilot
body: Driving a transit bus through city traffic gives you plenty of time to think about how different municipal departments operate. From a purely operational standpoint, I have mixed feelings about how staggered schedules will affect overall route coordination and public accessibility. However, looking at it from the perspective of human endurance, the four-day week will reduce burnout and improve employee morale and mental health. Driving tired people around all day makes you acutely aware of how critical adequate rest is for cognitive function. If municipal employees get that extra day to recover from their stressful routines, their overall psychological state should improve dramatically. Whether that offsets the administrative headaches of managing ten-hour shifts remains to be seen, but the mental health benefits for the staff are hard to ignore.

headline: About time municipal workers got a break
body: It is about time. The four-day week will reduce burnout and improve employee morale and mental health, which should be standard everywhere.

headline: Sure, let us see how ten-hour days work in reality
body: Oh yeah, because working ten-hour stretches on top of regular municipal bureaucracy is just a walk in the park. Everyone is acting like shaving off one day per week means workers are just lounging around sipping iced tea, completely ignoring the fact that those daily shifts just got a lot longer. Of course, the optimists keep insisting that the four-day week will reduce burnout and improve employee morale and mental health, as if fatigue magically disappears just because you get Friday off. Try telling that to the guys out in the field dealing with angry citizens and heavy workloads for extended hours. If people actually get more rest, great, but let us not pretend longer days do not take a massive physical and mental toll of their own.

headline: A necessary step to keep our workforce
body: When I knocked on doors during my council campaign, every department manager told me the same grim reality about staffing shortages. We hemorrhage talent to private tech firms and local corporations simply because municipal budgets cannot match their compensation packages. Offering a four-day schedule is a brilliant, zero-cost adjustment that fundamentally changes the value proposition for public servants. It will help the city recruit and retain staff, since it cannot compete with private-sector salaries.

headline: Economic realism in municipal hiring
body: From a strictly microeconomic perspective, the city faces a severe inelasticity problem regarding labor supply. Without matching the wage growth seen in the private sector over the last five years, traditional retention strategies are completely dead on arrival. Total compensation encompasses non-monetary benefits like schedule flexibility, which economic theory demonstrates can effectively offset lower take-home pay. By leveraging compressed workweeks, local government can partially bridge the widening compensation gap without raising taxes. It will help the city recruit and retain staff, since it cannot compete with private-sector salaries.

headline: Smart move for staffing
body: We cannot match corporate pay. This extra day off fixes that gap. It will help the city recruit and retain staff, since it cannot compete with private-sector salaries.

headline: Valuable incentive for public servants
body: In healthcare, we witness firsthand how critical scheduling flexibility is for mitigating severe occupational burnout and high turnover rates. Public administration faces an identical crisis, particularly when municipal coffers cannot match the aggressive salary structures offered by private healthcare and corporate entities. Introducing a compressed four-day model provides a highly desirable lifestyle benefit that makes public sector employment genuinely attractive. Ultimately, it will help the city recruit and retain staff, since it cannot compete with private-sector salaries.

headline: A practical tool for city hiring
body: As a working parent juggling three kids, I understand completely why professionals gravitate toward companies that offer better flexibility and perks. The city has always struggled to keep good people because corporate employers simply write bigger checks. Providing an extra day off each week creates an invaluable non-monetary incentive that balances out the lower public wages. It will help the city recruit and retain staff, since it cannot compete with private-sector salaries.

headline: Analyzing the labor market realities
body: Looking at the municipal labor market data over the past decade, it is clear that public sector wages lag far behind private enterprise benchmarks across nearly every administrative and technical category. Traditional recruitment drives fail repeatedly because prospective applicants quickly accept higher-paying positions in the private market. By shifting to a four-day format, the municipality introduces a strong compensating differential that alters cost-benefit calculations for job seekers. It will help the city recruit and retain staff, since it cannot compete with private-sector salaries.

headline: Why flexibility wins workers over
body: During my years representing workers, I watched countless dedicated employees walk out the door for private sector jobs offering higher hourly pay that the city budget could never touch. Workers want fair pay, but when public budgets are tight, lifestyle benefits make a massive difference in keeping morale high and turnover low. This new schedule introduces a tangible perk that makes staying in public service worthwhile for our members. It will help the city recruit and retain staff, since it cannot compete with private-sector salaries.

headline: Game changer for municipal workers
body: I cannot express how thrilled I am to see the council finally take a bold, progressive step to address our chronic department vacancies! For years, we have watched talented colleagues leave for private companies simply because those corporations can afford much higher wages. This incredible scheduling shift offers a wonderful quality-of-life benefit that makes up for the smaller paychecks we receive in local government. It will help the city recruit and retain staff, since it cannot compete with private-sector salaries.

headline: Addressing the municipal compensation gap
body: An evaluation of current municipal operating budgets demonstrates that direct wage parity with private industry is structurally impossible given statutory tax limitations. Therefore, leadership must utilize non-monetary compensation strategies to attract qualified candidates who might otherwise accept higher-paying corporate offers. Providing a compressed four-day operational schedule serves as an effective economic substitute for higher salaries by significantly reducing commuting costs and increasing personal time. It will help the city recruit and retain staff, since it cannot compete with private-sector salaries.

headline: Pilot program will severely bottleneck public access to municipal staff
body: As someone who navigates Riverton traffic daily, schedules matter. When operations shift to compressed hours, scheduling coordination breaks down. Data from transit logistics proves that reducing operational overlap compresses service windows. Residents will inevitably face slower response times and more difficulty reaching city offices and staff during critical operational hours. Staggered schedules sound fine on paper, but in practice, citizens trying to resolve civic issues on Fridays or late afternoons will hit a brick wall. The city cannot afford these bottlenecks.

headline: Good intentions, but citizens will pay the price with delays
body: During my campaign, I listened to hundreds of voters who already struggled to get prompt call-backs from city departments. When my neighbor tried to pull a simple zoning permit last year, it took weeks. Cutting into standard availability windows via ten-hour days will only exacerbate this. Even with staggered office coverage, residents will face slower response times and more difficulty reaching city offices and staff. We wanted modernization, but what we are getting is a logistical headache for ordinary taxpayers trying to get simple answers.

headline: Healthcare workers know longer hours lead to delays
body: In the ICU, fatigue changes everything. If city staff are working ten-hour days, exhaustion sets in, and efficiency drops. Consequently, residents will face slower response times and more difficulty reaching city offices and staff.

headline: Exciting trial, though scheduling hurdles are totally expected
body: It is awesome to see the city trying innovative scheduling models to boost morale! However, looking at this from a project management perspective, shrinking the active work week down to four days creates obvious logistical bumps. Even though leadership promises staggered desks, reality shows that fewer personnel on site simultaneously means bottlenecks. Therefore, residents will face slower response times and more difficulty reaching city offices and staff. I am pumped for the municipal workers getting extra rest, but let us be realistic about the customer service friction ahead.

headline: An economic assessment of service degradation under compressed municipal work schedules
body: From a purely economic standpoint, reducing the operational window of municipal bureaucracy inevitably introduces friction into transaction markets and public goods delivery. When the aggregate availability of municipal labor decreases relative to public demand, transactional costs for citizens rise. Even if total weekly hours theoretically balance out, the temporal concentration of personnel creates severe capacity constraints on peak days. Empirically, bottlenecking service hours leads directly to diminished municipal responsiveness. Consequently, residents will face slower response times and more difficulty reaching city offices and staff. While the theoretical appeal of increased employee retention is understandable, the macroeconomic trade-off involves a direct deterioration in public-facing utility and civic accessibility. Taxpayers fund these services expecting continuous administrative throughput, not artificially restricted communication channels that ultimately waste citizen time through prolonged bureaucratic latency.

headline: Formal analysis of administrative throughput and public accessibility trade-offs
body: The implementation of a compressed operational schedule for municipal personnel introduces significant structural variables regarding public accountability and agency responsiveness. While workforce satisfaction metrics are a legitimate administrative consideration, the primary mandate of local government remains the efficient delivery of services to the taxpaying public. When organizational units restructure their weekly availability—regardless of staggered administrative coverage—the density of incoming inquiries inevitably outpaces available staffing bandwidth during operational peaks. Historical data from analogous municipal transitions indicates that institutional friction rises proportionally with reduced day-to-day overlap. Therefore, residents will face slower response times and more difficulty reaching city offices and staff as administrative backlogs accumulate over the weekend closures. Stakeholders must carefully evaluate whether employee recruitment advantages outweigh the measurable decline in constituent accessibility, ensuring that accountability frameworks remain robust throughout this experimental one-year trial period.

headline: Riverton is completely ignoring the service delivery nightmare this pilot will cause
body: Managing human resources in the healthcare sector has taught me one absolute truth: operational changes that reduce daily availability always harm the end user. Riverton city leadership is living in a fantasy world if they think shrinking the standard operating week to four days will not utterly destroy customer service. When citizens need zoning permits, water billing adjustments, or code enforcement assistance, they need immediate answers—not a voicemail telling them the office is closed on a Friday or that the skeleton crew is overwhelmed. Despite all the polished talk about boosting employee morale and recruitment, the undeniable reality is that residents will face slower response times and more difficulty reaching city offices and staff. It is completely unacceptable that taxpayers are being asked to subsidize an administrative experiment that prioritizes staff convenience over public accountability. We already struggle to get timely municipal responses, and this pilot guarantees that civic bureaucracy will grind to an even more frustrating, sluggish halt.
persona: HR manager at a local hospital

headline: Excited for city workers, but worried about getting my questions answered
body: It is genuinely super cool that municipal employees are getting a three-day weekend out of this, because burnout is real and everyone deserves a better work-life balance! But as someone who constantly has to deal with local paperwork, I am kind of stressed about how this is going to play out in practice. Even though they promised that libraries and permit desks will have staggered schedules to stay open, a lot of departments are still going to be working behind closed doors on those compressed days. Honestly, it feels pretty obvious that residents will face slower response times and more difficulty reaching city offices and staff when trying to get urgent things sorted out. I am totally rooting for the city staff to enjoy their Fridays off, but I really hope local teenagers and families trying to access municipal resources do not end up completely stranded in endless phone trees and delayed email threads while trying to navigate this massive scheduling experiment.

headline: This Four-Day Work Week Will Just Cost Parents More
body: Oh wow, just fantastic news for our family budget! As a parent running around trying to keep up with three little kids, I was really hoping local government would find a shiny new way to squander our hard-earned dollars. Overtime costs are going to skyrocket because nobody can finish complex municipal projects in standard hours, and guess who gets to pay for all that extra payroll? You guessed it, folks! Taxpayers will end up footing the bill for this grand experiment while we struggle to pay for childcare and everything else. I just love how nobody consulted families about whether we want to finance longer weekends for city hall workers. Brilliant job, council members, truly stellar work looking out for the regular folks in this town!

headline: Association Volunteer Warns of Looming Overtime Expenses
body: In my years volunteering with the local taxpayer association, I have seen plenty of clever schemes dreamed up by bureaucrats, but this one takes the cake. Just last week, I was chatting with a neighbor who audited city expenditures, and we were shaking our heads over how predictable this cycle is. Whenever offices shift schedules without cutting total hours, scheduling gaps always emerge that require expensive shift coverage. Overtime costs will rise dramatically as departments scramble to cover peak service hours, and taxpayers will end up footing the bill for every single extra hour logged. History shows us that these pilot programs never save money; they only pad payrolls at the expense of fiscal responsibility and neighborhood wallets.

headline: Records Clerk Knows Overtime Will Cost Us Dearly
body: Working in records gives me a front-row seat to scheduling chaos. Overtime costs will rise because daily tasks routinely bleed past ten hours, and taxpayers will end up footing the bill for the extra pay.

headline: Economics Student Sees Budget Shortfalls Ahead
body: Studying local markets taught me that labor shifts without output gains destroy budgets. Overtime costs will rise exponentially, and taxpayers will end up footing the bill for these inefficiencies.

headline: Construction foreman looks at ten-hour shifts
body: Running crews on heavy jobsites taught me a long time ago that pushing past the eight-hour mark is where things start falling apart. Sure, a three-day weekend sounds great on paper, but I see firsthand how my guys start dragging around hour nine. Concentration drops off a cliff, and that is precisely when measuring mistakes happen or someone forgets to double-check a rigging line. I am torn because everyone deserves more rest, yet stretching the daily grind longer brings real safety risks. Ten-hour days are exhausting, and tired employees make more mistakes late in the shift. If city desk workers think shuffling paper for ten hours is a breeze, they are in for a rude awakening when the afternoon brain fog sets in.

headline: Bad idea for city hall
body: This pilot program is a major miscalculation by the council. Ten-hour days are exhausting, and tired employees make more mistakes late in the shift. Expect a sharp spike in administrative errors once the afternoon fatigue catches up to everyone.

headline: Bus driver perspective on long shifts
body: Navigating city traffic all day gives you a front-row seat to how human endurance fades. By the time the tenth hour rolls around, reaction times slow down dramatically no matter who you are. Ten-hour days are exhausting; tired employees make more mistakes late in the shift. While I understand why municipal workers want Fridays off, pushing the clock longer means dealing with distracted personnel when afternoon fatigue hits hardest. It is a gamble with public service quality.

headline: Healthcare worker warning on fatigue
body: Clinical data consistently demonstrates that extended shifts degrade cognitive performance. Ten-hour days are exhausting, and tired employees make more mistakes late in the shift. Municipal staff handling critical permits will inevitably experience reduced accuracy as fatigue accumulates.

headline: Economic oversight ignores working parents
body: From a purely logistical standpoint, the council's cost-benefit analysis completely overlooks the microeconomic strain on families. Shifting municipal operations to ten-hour shifts inevitably extends the workday until six in the evening. For any household with children, this structural adjustment directly violates standard school dismissal schedules and affordable childcare availability. Standard after-school programs rarely extend past five o'clock, leaving a critical gap in care that working parents cannot bridge without incurring severe financial penalties for late pickups or hiring private evening babysitters. If municipal labor models attempt to mimic corporate trends, they must account for the rigid constraints of scholastic timetables and domestic logistics. Without addressing this fundamental mismatch, the entire initiative fails basic utility testing for families.

headline: Oh great, another brilliant scheduling idea
body: Because ten-hour shifts seamlessly align with traditional elementary school hours and daycare closing times, right? Absolutely genius planning from folks who clearly have never tried to race across town at five-thirty for a school pickup while dealing with late afternoon traffic. Let us all just magically expand the continuum of time to accommodate municipal administrative convenience. Healthcare workers already juggle absurd shift rotations, but expecting standard parents to suddenly vanish from their desks ten hours later and materialize at the schoolyard is genuinely hilarious. If you enjoy paying exorbitant late fees to after-school programs because your permit office contact needed a longer weekend, you are in luck. Truly a masterclass in modern operational foresight that completely ignores basic domestic reality.

headline: Public health metrics ignore family logistics
body: It is fascinating how population-level policy proposals completely disregard the actual daily logistics of working parents. Extending daily shifts to ten hours creates an immediate collision with standard school dismissal schedules and childcare operating hours. Public health literature consistently demonstrates that parental stress spikes exponentially when rigid employment demands conflict with domestic care responsibilities. Expecting families to absorb an extra two hours of daily workplace presence without acknowledging the reality of school pickup times is remarkably short-sighted. Administrative wellness cannot come at the direct expense of household stability and logistical sanity. Until the city accounts for the actual hours children spend in school versus when parents are finally released from their desks, this pilot remains fundamentally flawed.

headline: Skeptical about how municipal output will truly be evaluated
body: As someone who spends their life analyzing public health outcomes and institutional metrics, I find the council's vague assurances deeply unsettling. What specific indicators will they use to determine if municipal workers are actually maintaining output across a compressed schedule? Are we talking about processing times, citizen satisfaction scores, or just internal surveys? Without rigorous, independently audited benchmarks, any numbers published by the city administration are practically worthless. Governments have a well-documented habit of framing internal pilot programs as massive successes regardless of the ground-level reality. If the administration wants the public to trust this massive operational shift, they need to release their entire evaluation framework right now, down to the raw data sets. Otherwise, residents are simply expected to take the city's word for it while services potentially degrade, and that is not how accountable local governance is supposed to function.

headline: Can we trust self-reported city data?
body: Working twelve-hour shifts in the ICU, I know burnout is real, but I still have to ask: how on earth are they going to measure productivity fairly? More importantly, can we actually trust the city to grade its own homework on this?

headline: Show us the real numbers
body: Running a downtown cafe means I care about how fast city permits get processed. How will productivity actually be measured here, and why should local business owners trust the city's self-reported data when they grade themselves?

headline: Finally, some common sense for our town's emissions
body: Oh sure, heaven forbid we try something that actually makes sense for once. As if juggling three kids under six wasn't already an extreme sport, I am supposed to weep over the tragedy of city hall using slightly less electricity one day a week. Let us be real here for a second. Having one fewer commute day per single week directly cuts down on vehicle emissions, which is fantastic for the air our kids have to breathe. On top of that, actually closing down some of these municipal buildings on the off day saves a massive amount of energy. But please, let us all clutch our pearls about how the bureaucrats might shuffle their hours instead of looking at the obvious environmental wins. Brilliant move, Riverton. Truly groundbreaking stuff.

headline: Must be nice to get a three day weekend
body: Oh, wonderful! As a downtown cafe owner working seventy hours a week on my feet without paid time off or special benefits, I am just thrilled that my tax dollars are funding a leisurely four day schedule for bureaucrats. Must be fantastic to enjoy three day weekends while small business owners struggle to keep their doors open. Who covers the extra costs when city hall is dark? Right, we do. Thanks for nothing.

headline: Four-day schedule will ease local traffic congestion
body: As someone who commutes past the municipal center daily during peak hours, I have analyzed the potential ripple effects of this council decision from a logistical standpoint. Even though the primary intent of the municipal pilot is to mitigate employee burnout and streamline recruitment, the secondary traffic implications are profoundly beneficial. By staggering the shifts for city personnel across different days of the week, the sheer volume of vehicles hitting the main corridors simultaneously will visibly disperse. Instead of every staff member arriving strictly between 8:00 and 8:30 AM, arrivals and departures will now be distributed across a broader temporal window. This dilution of rush-hour density directly minimizes roadway gridlock, lowers vehicular idling emissions, and makes the morning commute much smoother for all residents. From a strictly data-driven perspective on municipal flow dynamics, this schedule modification provides a clear ancillary advantage for our community's transportation infrastructure.

headline: A Four-Day Work Week Precedent Is Hard To Undoing
body: As a retired educator who spent decades navigating complex district policies and collective bargaining agreements, I find myself deeply conflicted regarding the municipal council's recent decision. While the prospect of enhanced staff morale and recruitment certainly holds theoretical appeal, experience dictates a more pragmatic caution. My primary concern rests not with the daily operational logistics during this upcoming twelve-month trial, but rather with the inevitable administrative permanence such a concession establishes. Once a benefit of this magnitude is formally integrated into municipal operations and presented to personnel, it becomes practically irreversible during subsequent union contract negotiations, regardless of what the quarterly productivity metrics or resident satisfaction surveys ultimately indicate. History demonstrates that labor concessions, once granted, are exceedingly difficult to retract when the trial period concludes. The city administration must recognize that they are not merely testing a temporary schedule change, but rather permanently altering the baseline expectations for municipal employment without a clear exit strategy for failure.

headline: City hall four-day schedule will hurt local downtown lunch spots
body: As someone who writes code from home all day, I rarely venture into the commercial district during the week, but I do notice the steady hum of commerce when I grab coffee on my occasional errands. When the municipality shifts its twelve hundred employees to a compressed schedule, those thousands of daily workers simply will not be walking out at noon to buy sandwiches, pastries, or retail items. From my vantage point behind a dual-monitor setup, local eateries depend heavily on that predictable rush of municipal foot traffic to survive thin margins. Cutting out a fifth of the operational week means businesses right around city hall face a sharp drop in reliable weekday revenue. While supporters focus on internal recruitment and reducing employee burnout, they are completely ignoring the collateral economic damage inflicted on small businesses that count on those steady lunch breaks to pay their rent and keep their doors open.

headline: This pilot program sounds like a really great idea overall.
body: Hey everyone, as an ICU nurse working crazy long shifts all the time, I honestly just think this whole new schedule is a good idea. Working in healthcare is exhausting, and hearing about Riverton trying this out makes me really happy. Honestly, I do not have much else to say about the logistics or the council vote details, but my gut feeling is just that it is a good idea for the staff. It is nice to see a local government try something positive for its workers for a change.

headline: Economic concerns regarding the municipal schedule adjustment.
body: From an analytical perspective, evaluating public sector operational shifts requires careful cost-benefit modeling, particularly regarding marginal productivity versus fixed overhead expenses. While labor supply elasticity in municipal hiring is a relevant factor, the potential for diminished citizen access during standard business hours introduces friction into the local economy. Ultimately, looking at the macro-level indicators and municipal budgetary constraints, this entire initiative strikes me fundamentally as a complete waste of money. Without rigorous empirical justification for altering baseline service delivery hours, taxpayers are left bearing the brunt of an unproven administrative experiment that lacks sufficient quantitative backing.

headline: Finally a positive change for the city workers.
body: Working behind the scenes in local government every single day is truly draining, so hearing about this upcoming shift in our schedule feels like a huge relief. People on the outside do not always realize how heavy the daily administrative workload gets, and getting that extra day off to recharge will make a massive difference in our overall well-being. Looking at the big picture, this trial period is simply a good idea for all of us trying to balance our jobs and personal lives. I am genuinely thrilled the council pushed this through despite the opposition.

headline: A critical assessment of the municipal scheduling change.
body: As a local business owner who depends heavily on predictable municipal services and responsive administrative offices, I must express serious reservations regarding the city council's recent vote. Local governance requires consistent availability to support commercial growth and maintain public infrastructure efficiently. Introducing staggered schedules and extended daily shifts risks creating bottlenecks in critical departments that local enterprises rely upon daily. Consequently, when weighing the purported benefits against the operational disruptions, this policy appears to be nothing more than a waste of money that ultimately fails to serve the best interests of the broader taxpaying community and local business owners.
